bib.title: Fundamentals of Deep Learning, Chapter 4: Beyond Gradient Descent
authors: Nikhil Buduma (book author; not printed in the chapter text)

question: Why does plain mini-batch gradient descent struggle on deep-network error surfaces, and which optimizers fix it?
contributions: Argues spurious local minima are exaggerated and saddle points and ill-conditioning are the real obstacles
Introduces momentum, second-order methods, AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam

results.claim: In a toy MNIST feed-forward net, momentum 0.9 at learning rate 0.01 reaches cost 0.1 in just over 2,000 minibatch steps versus nearly 18,000 without.
results.setup: MNIST feed-forward ReLU network from Ch. 3, TensorFlow MomentumOptimizer, learning_rate 0.01, momentum 0.9; single run read from TensorBoard curves
results.quote: requires nearly 18,000 steps (minibatches), whereas with momentum (left), we require just over 2,000.
results.note: Text says with-momentum is (left); the Fig 4-9 caption says with (right) and without (left). Left/right is inconsistent.

results.claim: A random critical point in d dimensions is a local minimum with probability 1/3^d, so local minima get exponentially rarer as parameters grow (heuristic assuming the three 1-D forms are equally likely).
results.setup: Heuristic: each of d axis slices is minimum, maximum or inflection with equal probability; the book defers rigour to Dauphin et al. 2014
results.quote: In other words, as the dimensionality of our parameter space increases, local minima become exponentially more rare.

results.claim: Linear interpolation from a random init to the SGD solution shows no troublesome local minima, so the difficulty is finding the direction, not getting stuck.
results.source: Goodfellow, Vinyals and Saxe 2014 (arXiv:1412.6544); the book reproduces it on its own MNIST net over alpha in [-2, 2) step 0.01 using test data
results.setup: Linear interpolation between random init and SGD solution, for a wide variety of practical networks
results.quote: we find that there are no truly troublesome local minima

results.claim: On elliptical contours the gradient can point 90 degrees from the direction of the minimum.
results.quote: the gradient can be as inaccurate as 90 degrees away from the correct direction!

results.claim: Adam defaults in TensorFlow are learning_rate 0.001, beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999, epsilon 1e-08; only the learning rate may need changing.
results.note: beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-08 are on the next line

results.claim: AdaGrad tends to drop the learning rate prematurely and works poorly for some deep models; RMSProp (decay 0.9, epsilon 1e-10 in the TF template) fixes this with an exponential moving average.

limits: No experiments beyond the toy MNIST MLP: single run, no seeds, no variance, no comparison between optimizers (a script is only pointed to).

Dated: TensorFlow 0.x API (placeholders, Session, tf.initialize_variables, SummaryWriter, xrange); says Nesterov, conjugate gradient and L-BFGS are not in TensorFlow; AdaDelta unsupported. All now available.

Dated: calls second-order methods unpopular and RMSProp a default for seasoned practitioners; says there is little consensus on optimizer choice. AdamW, weight decay decoupling, LR schedules and warmup are not covered.
The 1/3^d argument assumes the three 1-D critical point types are equally likely; the book admits this is loose.
Says it is an open question whether spurious local minima are common; the interpolation evidence is from Goodfellow et al. 2014.

Code snippets contain errors: random walk uses step_range=10 though text says -10 to 10 with a stray fused line; momentum_rand_walk.append() has no argument; the interpolated output layer applies relu to logits.
practices: Use momentum (typically 0.9) to damp oscillating gradients; it may need a reduced learning rate (p.75-76).
Prefer RMSProp or Adam over AdaGrad for deep nets; Adam defaults usually work and only the learning rate may need changing (p.80-82).
Do not expect optimizer choice to be the main lever; architecture that is easier to train has produced most breakthroughs (p.83).
Diagnose local minima by interpolating loss between init and trained weights, not by plotting loss over time (p.66-69).

a critical point that is neither minimum nor maximum, a flat region
